subject: maths
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the mode of a set of data?
options: The value that occurs most often
The middle value when in order
The difference between largest and smallest
The total divided by how many values
questions.explain: The mode is the most frequently occurring value in a data set.

questions.q: How is the median found?
options: It is the middle value when the data are arranged in order
It is the most common value
It is the sum of all values divided by the number of values
It is the largest value minus the smallest value
questions.explain: The median is the central value once the data are placed in ascending (or descending) order.

questions.q: The range of a data set is calculated by:
options: Dividing the total by the number of values
questions.explain: The range is a measure of spread found by subtracting the smallest value from the largest.

questions.q: Find the mean of 4, 7, 9, 10 and 5.
questions.explain: The values sum to 35, and 35 divided by 5 gives a mean of 7.

questions.q: Find the median of 3, 8, 5, 9, 2 and 7.
questions.explain: Ordered they are 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9; the median is the mean of the two middle values, (5+7)/2 = 6.

questions.q: On the probability scale, all probabilities must lie between:
questions.explain: A probability of 0 means impossible and 1 means certain, so all values fall between 0 and 1 inclusive.

questions.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability that it does not rain?
For a set of mutually exclusive outcomes that cover every possibility, the probabilities must add up to:
questions.explain: The probabilities of all possible mutually exclusive outcomes always sum to 1.

questions.q: A fair six-sided dice is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an even number?
questions.explain: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, giving 3 out of 6 outcomes, which simplifies to 1/2.

questions.q: On a histogram with unequal class widths, the frequency density is found by:
questions.explain: For a histogram the vertical axis shows frequency density = frequency / class width.

questions.q: To find the angle for a category in a pie chart, you calculate:
questions.explain: A full pie chart is 360 degrees, so each category's angle is its fraction of the total multiplied by 360.

questions.q: A scatter graph shows that as one variable increases, the other also increases. This indicates:
questions.explain: When both variables increase together the points trend upwards, showing positive correlation.

questions.q: A straight line drawn through the trend of points on a scatter graph is called:
questions.explain: A line of best fit summarises the trend of the data and can be used to make estimates.

questions.q: Which situation is most likely to show negative correlation?
options: The age of a car and its value
A person's height and their shoe size
The temperature and the number of ice creams sold
The number of pages and the thickness of a book
questions.explain: As a car gets older its value tends to fall, giving negative correlation.

questions.q: In a simple random sample of a population:
options: Every member has an equal chance of being selected
Members are chosen in fixed groups
The first available people are chosen
questions.explain: A random sample gives each member of the population an equal chance of selection, reducing bias.

questions.q: A stratified sample is one in which:
options: The population is divided into groups and each is sampled in proportion to its size
Only the largest group is sampled
People are chosen at regular intervals from a list
Every member of the population is surveyed
questions.explain: Stratified sampling splits the population into strata and samples each in proportion to its size.

questions.q: The interquartile range (IQR) is calculated as:
questions.explain: The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data and equals UQ - LQ.

questions.q: Relative frequency from an experiment is used to:
options: Estimate the probability of an event
Calculate the mean of the data
Draw a line of best fit
questions.explain: Relative frequency (successes divided by number of trials) gives an experimental estimate of probability.

questions.q: A fair dice is rolled 60 times. How many sixes would you expect?
questions.explain: Expected frequency = probability x number of trials = (1/6) x 60 = 10.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of continuous data?
options: The heights of pupils in a class
The number of pupils in each class
The shoe sizes sold in a shop
The number of goals scored in matches
questions.explain: Continuous data can take any value within a range and are measured, such as height.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Mathematics (2017) specification; Handling Data
